claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists as a high-temperature, single-phase disordered BCC alloy.
Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a thermodynamic drive for short-range ordering and configurational entropy.
The proposed short-range ordering preferentially involves Al and transition-metal atoms.
Cr modifies the interatomic interaction energies that control ordering in this alloy.
At elevated temperature, configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered BCC state against ordering.
Reducing temperature allows the thermodynamic driving force from specific interatomic interactions to dominate over entropic stabilization.
Lower-temperature annealing will induce local chemical ordering and nucleation of ordered B2 domains within the BCC matrix.
Preferential Al–transition-metal pairing mediates the formation and growth of B2 domains.
Sluggish diffusion competes with the thermodynamic ordering drive, and their balance determines observed phase stability.
Annealing below the high-temperature stability regime will progressively produce ordered B2 domains in the disordered BCC matrix.
The B2 phase fraction will increase upon further cooling.
The size of B2 regions will increase upon further cooling.
Cooling will transform the alloy from single-phase BCC into a B2 plus BCC two-phase mixture.
A lower-Cr Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloy or related AlCoFeNi alloy should exhibit a more stable high-temperature single phase or different ordering behavior under similar treatments.
Prior work found single-phase ordered B2 AlCoFeNi at high temperature and found that replacing Co with Cr and lowering annealing temperature favored B2 plus BCC decomposition.
The length scale of B2 plus BCC decomposition depends on alloy composition and annealing temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies only where diffusion is sufficiently active for ordering but before extensive grain growth or coarsening.
At sufficiently high temperature, entropic stabilization dominates ordering.
At very low temperature, kinetic arrest or secondary precipitation may obscure the proposed ordering mechanism.
Failure to detect B2 domains after controlled annealing in the predicted regime, or failure of phase evolution to correlate with reduced temperature and local ordering, would falsify the hypothesis.
